content.content:
1	Equipment is frequently attached to the outside of a pipe after the pipe has been installed. Sensors, small tools, brackets, and lengths of conduit all have to be carried on a pipe that cannot be taken out of service, cannot be lifted, and has no free end over which a closed ring could be threaded. A clamp intended for that duty therefore has to open from the side, close around the pipe, and grip it firmly enough that the carried equipment keeps its position, while remaining removable so that the same clamp can be taken off and used again elsewhere.
2	
3	A clamp that opens from the side is split into parts, and the split is what makes the gripping problem difficult. Once the clamp body is divided, any drive element that runs around the body is divided with it. Gripping arrangements that answer this by driving the gripping surfaces of each part separately give up the fixed relationship between the two parts of the drive: the two sides of the clamp advance by amounts that depend on how each side is operated, so the clamp tends to settle off center on the pipe, and the load is shared unevenly between the gripping surfaces. Arrangements that instead pull the split body closed on the pipe, in the manner of a band or a two-bolt saddle, transfer the closing force through the joint at the split and rely on the pipe itself to react the closing motion, so the grip depends on how nearly the bore of the clamp matches the outside diameter of the pipe. Such an arrangement is commonly supplied with liners or inserts machined for one nominal pipe size, and a different pipe size calls for a different insert or a different clamp.
4	
5	Reusable clamping also has to deal with the force the operator applies. A hand lever gives the operator no measure of what has been done to the pipe. When the gripping elements have reached the pipe, further travel of the lever has to go somewhere, and in a rigid drive train it goes into whichever gripping element happens to touch first, so that one gripping surface is loaded far more than the others. Thin walled tube, coated pipe, and lined pipe are all damaged by that kind of concentrated loading, and the operator has no indication that it has occurred. Torque tools and gauges can be added to the installation, but they add a separate instrument to the task and, when they respond to the position of the gripping elements, they report the size of the pipe rather than the force in the grip.
6	
7	What has been lacking is a split clamp in which the drive that advances the gripping elements is itself restored to a single, continuous element by the act of closing the clamp, in which every gripping element is advanced from that one drive so that the gripping elements advance together over a range of pipe sizes, and in which the travel remaining in the operator's lever after the gripping elements have landed on the pipe is absorbed within the clamp and reported to the operator as a loading condition rather than as a dimension.
8

1	The following description of embodiments refers to the accompanying drawings. The same reference numeral denotes the same part throughout. Terms of direction are used with respect to the frame of the clamp: the axis of the frame is the axis about which the frame is annular in the closed condition, "inward" and "radially inward" mean toward that axis, "outward" and "radially outward" mean away from it, and "circumferential" means about that axis. These terms describe relationships within the clamp and do not require the clamp to be used in any particular attitude.
2	
3	Overall arrangement
4	
5	FIG. 1 shows a split pipe clamp 100 in the closed condition around a pipe 90. The clamp 100 has a first frame half 10 and a second frame half 12. Each of the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 is semicircular, and the two frame halves together surround the pipe 90. The first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 are joined at one end, referred to as the hinge end, by a hinge 14, and are releasably joined at the other end, referred to as the latch end, by a releasable latch 16. The hinge 14 permits the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 to be swung apart far enough for the clamp 100 to be passed sideways onto a pipe 90 that is already installed, so that the clamp 100 need not be threaded over a free end of the pipe 90. When the frame halves are brought together and the latch 16 is engaged, the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 define a frame that is annular about the axis of the clamp 100.
6	
7	Three jaw carriages 30 are distributed around the frame in the closed condition, so that the three jaw carriages 30 approach the pipe 90 from three different directions. Each jaw carriage 30 moves radially with respect to the frame and carries at its inner end a jaw pad 40, which is described below in connection with FIG. 3. The jaw pads 40 carried at the inner ends of the three jaw carriages 30 bear on the pipe 90 when the clamp 100 is clamped. The clamp 100 does not require an insert dimensioned to a particular pipe diameter, and the same clamp 100 serves pipes of different diameters within the radial travel of the jaw carriages 30.
8	
9	The frame may carry a mounting boss 70 outside the annular guide 18 described below, as shown in FIG. 5. The mounting boss 70 supports a sensor, a tool, or a conduit that is to be held on the pipe 90 by the clamp 100. The mounting boss 70 is connected neither to the segmented cam ring 20 nor to any jaw carriage 30 and does not participate in the synchronization of the jaw carriages 30. Equipment carried at the mounting boss 70 therefore lies outside the drive path by which the jaws are advanced. The mounting boss 70 is an optional feature of the clamp 100 and may be omitted.
10	
11	The segmented cam ring
12	
13	FIG. 2 shows the segmented cam ring 20 of the clamp 100, drawn removed from the frame with its segments in the coupled condition. The segmented cam ring 20 comprises a first cam ring segment 22 and a second cam ring segment 24. The first cam ring segment 22 is carried by the first frame half 10 and the second cam ring segment 24 is carried by the second frame half 12, so that each frame half carries one segment of the ring and each segment travels with its own frame half when the clamp 100 is opened.
14	
15	The first cam ring segment 22 and the second cam ring segment 24 meet at two places, one at the hinge end and one at the latch end. At the hinge end the two segments have complementary coupling faces 26, and at the latch end they have complementary coupling faces 28. The complementary coupling faces 26 and the complementary coupling faces 28 are circumferentially facing drive faces, each pair being shaped so that one segment can transmit circumferential force to the other through the joint. The faces are brought into engagement by the same motion that closes the frame halves: as the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 are swung together about the hinge 14 and the latch 16 is engaged, the complementary coupling faces 26 close on one another at the hinge end and the complementary coupling faces 28 close on one another at the latch end.
16	
17	Coupling the segments in this way solves a problem created by splitting the clamp. A clamp that must open from the side cannot carry a continuous drive ring across the split, and a divided drive must otherwise be operated separately in each half, with the result that the two halves advance their jaws by amounts that are not fixed relative to one another. Here the division of the ring is undone by the act of closing the clamp. In the closed condition the first cam ring segment 22 and the second cam ring segment 24 are coupled at both ends and rotate together in the annular guide as a coupled ring, and a circumferential input applied to either segment is carried around the whole ring. One input, applied at one point on one frame half, therefore reaches every jaw carriage 30 through a single kinematic element, and the relationship between the jaw carriages 30 is set by the geometry of the ring rather than by the way the clamp is operated. When the latch 16 is released and the frame halves are swung apart, the complementary coupling faces 26 and the complementary coupling faces 28 separate and each segment stays with its own frame half, so that the coupling is made and broken by the closing and opening of the frame halves.
18	
19	The segmented cam ring 20 has three oblique slots 34, one for each jaw carriage 30. Each oblique slot 34 is inclined to the radial direction of the frame at the circumferential position of that slot, so that rotation of the coupled ring produces inward travel of its jaw carriage 30, the three oblique slots 34 being arranged so that the three jaw carriages 30 travel inwardly in synchronism. The inclination of the oblique slots 34 sets the ratio between the circumferential stroke of the coupled ring and the radial travel of the jaw carriages 30.
20	
21	The segmented cam ring 20 further has a ring drive face 36, shown in FIG. 2 at the latch end of the ring, against which the latch acts as described below. The ring drive face 36 is presented at a position on the ring that the wedge of the latch can reach, and it lies at an inclination to the direction in which that wedge advances, so that advance of the wedge moves the segmented cam ring 20 circumferentially.
22	
23	The jaw carriages
24	
25	FIG. 3 is a fragmentary sectional view through one jaw carriage 30, taken along line 3-3 of FIG. 1. The frame is channeled to form the annular guide 18, which receives the segmented cam ring 20. The annular guide 18 retains the first cam ring segment 22 on the first frame half 10 and the second cam ring segment 24 on the second frame half 12, and permits the coupled ring to move circumferentially.
26	
27	The frame is further formed with a radial guide 38 at the position of each jaw carriage 30. Each jaw carriage 30 is received in a respective radial guide 38 and is constrained by the radial guide 38 to move radially with respect to the frame. Each jaw carriage 30 carries a follower 32 that projects from the jaw carriage 30 into a respective one of the oblique slots 34 of the segmented cam ring 20. The follower 32 bears against the sides of the oblique slot 34.
28	
29	The follower 32 is constrained in two ways at once. The radial guide 38 prevents the jaw carriage 30, and therefore the follower 32, from moving circumferentially, while the oblique slot 34 holds the follower 32 at a position along the slot, which is inclined to the radial direction, so that circumferential movement of the segmented cam ring 20 displaces the follower 32 radially. When the coupled ring turns through its stroke, the side of each oblique slot 34 bears on the corresponding follower 32 and drives it, and with it the jaw carriage 30, radially inward along the radial guide 38. Because all three followers 32 are engaged in oblique slots 34 of one coupled ring, the three jaw carriages 30 advance inwardly in synchronism for as long as the ring turns. The jaw pads 40 therefore close on the pipe together.
30

The following description of embodiments refers to the accompanying drawings. The same reference numeral denotes the same part throughout. Terms of direction are used with respect to the frame of the clamp: the axis of the frame is the axis about which the frame is annular in the closed condition, "inward" and "radially inward" mean toward that axis, "outward" and "radially outward" mean away from it, and "circumferential" means about that axis. These terms describe relationships within the clamp and do not require the clamp to be used in any particular attitude.

Overall arrangement

FIG. 1 shows a split pipe clamp 100 in the closed condition around a pipe 90. The clamp 100 has a first frame half 10 and a second frame half 12. Each of the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 is semicircular, and the two frame halves together surround the pipe 90. The first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 are joined at one end, referred to as the hinge end, by a hinge 14, and are releasably joined at the other end, referred to as the latch end, by a releasable latch 16. The hinge 14 permits the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 to be swung apart far enough for the clamp 100 to be passed sideways onto a pipe 90 that is already installed, so that the clamp 100 need not be threaded over a free end of the pipe 90. When the frame halves are brought together and the latch 16 is engaged, the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 define a frame that is annular about the axis of the clamp 100.

Three jaw carriages 30 are distributed around the frame in the closed condition, so that the three jaw carriages 30 approach the pipe 90 from three different directions. Each jaw carriage 30 moves radially with respect to the frame and carries at its inner end a jaw pad 40, which is described below in connection with FIG. 3. The jaw pads 40 carried at the inner ends of the three jaw carriages 30 bear on the pipe 90 when the clamp 100 is clamped. The clamp 100 does not require an insert dimensioned to a particular pipe diameter, and the same clamp 100 serves pipes of different diameters within the radial travel of the jaw carriages 30.

The frame may carry a mounting boss 70 outside the annular guide 18 described below, as shown in FIG. 5. The mounting boss 70 supports a sensor, a tool, or a conduit that is to be held on the pipe 90 by the clamp 100. The mounting boss 70 is connected neither to the segmented cam ring 20 nor to any jaw carriage 30 and does not participate in the synchronization of the jaw carriages 30. Equipment carried at the mounting boss 70 therefore lies outside the drive path by which the jaws are advanced. The mounting boss 70 is an optional feature of the clamp 100 and may be omitted.

The segmented cam ring

FIG. 2 shows the segmented cam ring 20 of the clamp 100, drawn removed from the frame with its segments in the coupled condition. The segmented cam ring 20 comprises a first cam ring segment 22 and a second cam ring segment 24. The first cam ring segment 22 is carried by the first frame half 10 and the second cam ring segment 24 is carried by the second frame half 12, so that each frame half carries one segment of the ring and each segment travels with its own frame half when the clamp 100 is opened.

The first cam ring segment 22 and the second cam ring segment 24 meet at two places, one at the hinge end and one at the latch end. At the hinge end the two segments have complementary coupling faces 26, and at the latch end they have complementary coupling faces 28. The complementary coupling faces 26 and the complementary coupling faces 28 are circumferentially facing drive faces, each pair being shaped so that one segment can transmit circumferential force to the other through the joint. The faces are brought into engagement by the same motion that closes the frame halves: as the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 are swung together about the hinge 14 and the latch 16 is engaged, the complementary coupling faces 26 close on one another at the hinge end and the complementary coupling faces 28 close on one another at the latch end.

Coupling the segments in this way solves a problem created by splitting the clamp. A clamp that must open from the side cannot carry a continuous drive ring across the split, and a divided drive must otherwise be operated separately in each half, with the result that the two halves advance their jaws by amounts that are not fixed relative to one another. Here the division of the ring is undone by the act of closing the clamp. In the closed condition the first cam ring segment 22 and the second cam ring segment 24 are coupled at both ends and rotate together in the annular guide as a coupled ring, and a circumferential input applied to either segment is carried around the whole ring. One input, applied at one point on one frame half, therefore reaches every jaw carriage 30 through a single kinematic element, and the relationship between the jaw carriages 30 is set by the geometry of the ring rather than by the way the clamp is operated. When the latch 16 is released and the frame halves are swung apart, the complementary coupling faces 26 and the complementary coupling faces 28 separate and each segment stays with its own frame half, so that the coupling is made and broken by the closing and opening of the frame halves.

The segmented cam ring 20 has three oblique slots 34, one for each jaw carriage 30. Each oblique slot 34 is inclined to the radial direction of the frame at the circumferential position of that slot, so that rotation of the coupled ring produces inward travel of its jaw carriage 30, the three oblique slots 34 being arranged so that the three jaw carriages 30 travel inwardly in synchronism. The inclination of the oblique slots 34 sets the ratio between the circumferential stroke of the coupled ring and the radial travel of the jaw carriages 30.

The segmented cam ring 20 further has a ring drive face 36, shown in FIG. 2 at the latch end of the ring, against which the latch acts as described below. The ring drive face 36 is presented at a position on the ring that the wedge of the latch can reach, and it lies at an inclination to the direction in which that wedge advances, so that advance of the wedge moves the segmented cam ring 20 circumferentially.

The jaw carriages

FIG. 3 is a fragmentary sectional view through one jaw carriage 30, taken along line 3-3 of FIG. 1. The frame is channeled to form the annular guide 18, which receives the segmented cam ring 20. The annular guide 18 retains the first cam ring segment 22 on the first frame half 10 and the second cam ring segment 24 on the second frame half 12, and permits the coupled ring to move circumferentially.

The frame is further formed with a radial guide 38 at the position of each jaw carriage 30. Each jaw carriage 30 is received in a respective radial guide 38 and is constrained by the radial guide 38 to move radially with respect to the frame. Each jaw carriage 30 carries a follower 32 that projects from the jaw carriage 30 into a respective one of the oblique slots 34 of the segmented cam ring 20. The follower 32 bears against the sides of the oblique slot 34.

The follower 32 is constrained in two ways at once. The radial guide 38 prevents the jaw carriage 30, and therefore the follower 32, from moving circumferentially, while the oblique slot 34 holds the follower 32 at a position along the slot, which is inclined to the radial direction, so that circumferential movement of the segmented cam ring 20 displaces the follower 32 radially. When the coupled ring turns through its stroke, the side of each oblique slot 34 bears on the corresponding follower 32 and drives it, and with it the jaw carriage 30, radially inward along the radial guide 38. Because all three followers 32 are engaged in oblique slots 34 of one coupled ring, the three jaw carriages 30 advance inwardly in synchronism for as long as the ring turns. The jaw pads 40 therefore close on the pipe together.

At its inner end each jaw carriage 30 carries a jaw pad 40. The jaw pad 40 is pivotally mounted on the jaw carriage 30 and has a concave bearing face directed inwardly of the frame. Because the jaw pad 40 is free to pivot on the jaw carriage 30, the concave bearing face aligns itself with the outer surface of the pipe as it lands. The same concave bearing face therefore seats on pipes of different diameters, and no insert dimensioned to a particular pipe diameter is required.

A carriage return spring 44 acts between each jaw carriage 30 and the frame so as to urge that jaw carriage 30 radially outward. When the latch 16 is released and the drive from the latch to the ring drive face 36 is removed, the carriage return springs 44 push the jaw carriages 30 outward and the jaw pads 40 are retracted from the pipe, and the clamp 100 is left with its jaw carriages 30 retracted and ready for the next installation. Retraction of the jaw carriages 30 clears the jaw pads 40 from the pipe before the frame halves are swung apart.

The latch and the force-limiting drive train

FIG. 4 shows the latch 16 in fragmentary section. The latch 16 includes a latch housing 58 mounted on the frame at the latch end, a latch handle 50 pivotally mounted on the latch housing 58, a wedge 52 movable in the latch housing 58, and a force-limiting spring stack 54 in the drive train between the latch handle 50 and the wedge 52. The wedge 52 is positioned so that its inclined face bears on the ring drive face 36 of the segmented cam ring 20.

The latch 16 has two engaged positions. In a first position, the latch 16 holds the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 closed around the pipe 90 but does not clamp it: the frame is captive on the pipe 90 and cannot fall away, while the jaw carriages 30 remain retracted under their carriage return springs 44. In a second, over-center position, the wedge 52 drives the segmented cam ring 20 and the pipe 90 is clamped. Movement of the latch handle 50 from the first position to the second position advances the wedge 52 against the ring drive face 36. The inclined face of the wedge 52 converts that advance into circumferential movement of the segmented cam ring 20, and the coupled ring turns through its limited stroke.

The force-limiting spring stack 54 answers the problem of what becomes of the operator's remaining handle travel. The jaw pads 40 land on the pipe 90 at some point in the stroke that depends on the diameter of the pipe 90, and the latch handle 50 has still to be carried into its over-center position. If the drive train from the latch handle 50 to the wedge 52 were rigid, that remaining travel would be taken up by whatever part of the assembly yielded first, in practice by driving one jaw farther into the pipe 90 than the others and loading it far more heavily. Additional travel of the latch handle 50 after all three jaw pads 40 have contacted the pipe 90 compresses the force-limiting spring stack 54 rather than forcing one jaw carriage 30 farther inward than the others.

An indicator pin 56 is coupled to the force-limiting spring stack 54 and projects from the latch housing 58. As the force-limiting spring stack 54 compresses, the indicator pin 56 moves relative to a fixed edge of the latch housing 58, and the position of the indicator pin 56 with respect to that fixed edge shows the operator when the force-limiting spring stack 54 has entered a predetermined compression range. The predetermined compression range is the range of stack compression that corresponds to the clamping force for which the clamp 100 is intended. The indicator pin 56 therefore reports clamp loading mechanically, and what it reports is the state of the force-limiting spring stack 54. It is not a measurement of the diameter of the pipe 90.

Operation

To install the clamp 100 on a pipe 90, the operator opens the latch 16 and swings the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 apart about the hinge 14. The first cam ring segment 22 stays with the first frame half 10 and the second cam ring segment 24 stays with the second frame half 12, and the complementary coupling faces 26 and the complementary coupling faces 28 are separated. The operator places the frame halves around the pipe 90 from the side and closes them about the hinge 14. Closing the frame halves brings the complementary coupling faces 26 into engagement at the hinge end and the complementary coupling faces 28 into engagement at the latch end, coupling the first cam ring segment 22 and the second cam ring segment 24 into the coupled ring within the annular guide 18.

The operator then moves the latch 16 to its first position, in which the frame is held around the pipe 90 without clamping. The operator moves the latch handle 50 to the second, over-center position. The wedge 52 is driven against the ring drive face 36, the coupled ring turns through its stroke, the sides of the three oblique slots 34 drive the three followers 32, and the three jaw carriages 30 advance inwardly in synchronism until the pivoting jaw pads 40 seat on the pipe 90. The remaining travel of the latch handle 50 compresses the force-limiting spring stack 54, and the operator watches the indicator pin 56 move relative to the fixed edge of the latch housing 58 and so sees that the force-limiting spring stack 54 has entered the predetermined compression range. The latch 16 is left in the over-center position and the clamp 100 is loaded on the pipe 90.

To remove the clamp 100, the operator releases the latch 16. The latch handle 50 comes back over center, the wedge 52 retreats from the ring drive face 36, and the force-limiting spring stack 54 is unloaded. The carriage return springs 44 then push the jaw carriages 30 radially outward, so that the jaw pads 40 lift from the pipe 90. Only then are the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 swung apart about the hinge 14 and the clamp 100 taken off the pipe 90. The clamp 100 is undamaged by the cycle and may be installed again on the same pipe or on a pipe of a different diameter within the radial travel of the jaw carriages 30.

Features described above in connection with one embodiment may be combined with features described in connection with another, except where the context makes the combination impossible. The embodiments described are illustrative of the disclosed clamp and are not exhaustive of it, and the scope of protection is defined by the claims that follow rather than by any particular embodiment described here.

content.text: I've read all inputs, all ten draft sections, the numeral table, and all five figure briefs, and traced every claim limitation, numbered part, and figure element against the disclosure and the single USER passage in the conversation.

input.summary: Source-fidelity preflight v7 complete. The disclosure and the single USER turn in conversation.md are identical in substance, and they support the great majority of the draft: the two semicircular frame halves, hinge and releasable latch, three radial jaw carriages in radial guides, pivoting concave jaw pads that need no diameter-specific insert, the segmented cam ring retained in an annular guide with one segment per half, the complementary hinge-end and latch-end coupling faces that couple on closing, followers in three oblique slots producing synchronized inward travel, the wedge acting on a ring drive face, the limited stroke, the outward-biasing carriage springs, the first (holding) and second (over-center) latch positions, the force-limiting spring stack between handle and wedge, the indicator pin moving relative to a fixed edge of the latch housing over a predetermined compression range, the express statement that the indicator reports loading and not pipe diameter, the optional mounting boss outside the annular guide for a sensor/tool/conduit and its non-participation in synchronization, and both the installation and removal sequences. Claims 1-15 (apparatus, pipe-mounted equipment assembly, and method) each trace to affirmative disclosure text; the numeral table is complete, one-to-one, and every numeral used in the description and briefs is listed; no drafting notes, placeholders, or open questions remain; title, cross-reference, and government-support sections match the brief (no priority claim, no federal funding). Background prior-art characterizations were not traced, per instruction. Six issues remain, all in the figure briefs or in one derived claim/description phrase: one substantive kinematic contradiction in the FIG. 4 indicator-pin arrangement, one muddled FIG. 4 annular-guide description that also disagrees with FIGS. 3 and 5, an undisclosed and unlabeled handle-to-spring-seat linkage, an inferred "carriages retracted" state recited in three claims, and two unsupported proportion choices not marked schematic. Every finding has a concrete, filing-clean fix confined to the file where the problem lives.

findings.title: FIG. 4 mounts the indicator pin on the handle-driven spring seat, so the pin reports handle position rather than spring-stack compression
findings.where: figures/FIG-4.md lines 13 and 15; draft/08-detailed-description.md line 43; draft/09-claims.md claims 2, 3, 11, 14
findings.detail: The FIG. 4 brief pivots the latch handle 50 rigidly to the latch housing 58 and has "a short arm ... press[] down on the flat plate", and then rises the indicator pin 56 from that same flat plate. Because the arm and pivot are rigid and housing-mounted, the height of the flat plate relative to the fixed housing is fixed by the handle angle alone; the compression of the force-limiting spring stack 54 (which lies below the plate, between the plate and the wedge 52) does not displace the plate relative to the housing at all. The pin as briefed therefore cannot perform the function the description and claims assign to it. This contradicts the description's "As the force-limiting spring stack 54 compresses, the indicator pin 56 moves relative to a fixed edge of the latch housing 58", claim 2's "movable relative to a fixed edge of the latch housing when the force-limiting spring stack enters a predetermined compression range", and claim 3's "displaced by compression of the force-limiting spring stack independently of a diameter of the pipe". The inventor disclosed the reported behavior but not the linkage geometry, so the contradiction is introduced by the brief, not by the source.
findings.evidence: figures/FIG-4.md: "A short arm reaches from that pivot down and to the left and presses down on the flat plate at a point spaced from the pivot." and "A slender pin, the indicator pin 56, rises from the flat plate through a hole in the top wall of the latch housing 58 and stands above it." vs. draft/08-detailed-description.md line 43: "As the force-limiting spring stack 54 compresses, the indicator pin 56 moves relative to a fixed edge of the latch housing 58". Nearest source passage: disclosure.md line 9: "A visible indicator pin moves relative to a fixed edge of the latch housing when the spring stack enters a predetermined compression range." — the disclosure states the behavior and the reference edge, and says nothing about which member of the drive train the pin rises from.
findings.fix: In figures/FIG-4.md, replace the indicator-pin sentence with: "A slender pin, the indicator pin 56, is coupled to the force-limiting spring stack 54 and rises through a hole in the top wall of the latch housing 58 to stand above it; its coupling to the force-limiting spring stack 54 is shown schematically." Leave draft/08-detailed-description.md and the claims unchanged.

findings.title: FIG. 4 describes the annular guide both as a channel open radially outward and as material broken away, and disagrees with FIGS. 3 and 5
findings.where: figures/FIG-4.md line 5; figures/FIG-3.md lines 6-8; figures/FIG-5.md line 5
findings.detail: FIG. 4 says the body has "a channel in its upper face" holding the cam ring band and, in the same sentence, that "the frame is broken away above the band, exposing its upper side". If the band sits in a channel in the upper face there is no frame material above it to break away, so the two clauses cannot both be true. The clause also conflicts with FIGS. 3 and 5, which both show the annular guide 18 as a groove "bounded by the body above and below" and open in the axial direction, i.e. with frame material radially outside the cam ring. One depiction of the annular guide must serve all three figures.
findings.evidence: figures/FIG-4.md line 5: "a channel in its upper face holds a hatched arcuate band, the segmented cam ring 20, running from the left edge toward the middle, and the frame is broken away above the band, exposing its upper side" vs. figures/FIG-3.md line 7: "The groove is wider than deep, bounded by the body above and below, closed at its right and open toward the left. That groove is the annular guide 18." and figures/FIG-5.md line 5: "bounded by the body on its radially outer side above and its radially inner side below".
findings.fix: In figures/FIG-4.md, replace the clause with: "the body holds a hatched arcuate band, the segmented cam ring 20, running from the left edge toward the middle, the frame being broken away above the band so that its upper side is exposed".

findings.title: FIG. 4 specifies an undisclosed handle-arm-to-spring-seat linkage without labelling it schematic
findings.detail: The brief fixes a particular linkage topology and lever geometry between the latch handle and the force-limiting spring stack: the handle is pivoted to the housing at a stated location and a short arm reaches from that pivot "down and to the left" to press on the spring seat "at a point spaced from the pivot". A point of application spaced from the pivot sets a lever ratio and therefore conveys technical substance (how much force the handle delivers to the stack). The disclosure states only that the stack "lies between the latch handle and the wedge" and never describes the connecting linkage. The brief's schematic list covers only "the flat plate ... the latch housing, its cavity, and the gap through which the latch handle 50 passes", so this linkage is not within the depiction-convention safe harbor.
findings.evidence: figures/FIG-4.md line 13: "An elongated lever, the latch handle 50, is pivoted to the latch housing 58 at a small circle at the upper right of the cavity. A short arm reaches from that pivot down and to the left and presses down on the flat plate at a point spaced from the pivot." Nearest source passage: disclosure.md line 9: "A force-limiting spring stack lies between the latch handle and the wedge, so that additional handle travel after all jaw pads contact the pipe compresses the spring stack rather than forcing one jaw farther than the others." — no affirmative passage describes any handle pivot location, arm, or point of application.
findings.fix: In figures/FIG-4.md line 3, extend the schematic list to read: "The flat plate is a spring seat, and the latch housing, its cavity, the gap through which the latch handle 50 passes, and the linkage by which the latch handle 50 acts on the flat plate are shown schematically." Add "; that linkage is shown schematically" at the end of the short-arm sentence in line 13.

findings.title: "Jaw carriages retracted" in the first latch position is inferred, not affirmatively disclosed
findings.detail: Claims 4 and 12 recite a first latch position "in which the first frame half and the second frame half are held closed around the pipe received in the frame with the jaw carriages retracted", claim 13 recites moving the latch "to a first position in which the first frame half and the second frame half are held around the pipe with three jaw carriages of the split pipe clamp retracted", and the description states the carriages "remain retracted under their carriage return springs 44". The disclosure characterises the first position only as holding the halves "around the pipe without clamping", and states the outward bias only for the released condition ("A spring biases each carriage outward when the latch is released"), which is not the first engaged position. The retracted state is a plausible consequence of the disclosed structure but is not stated anywhere in the source, and reciting it in three claims narrows them on an unstated condition.
